newsitem.title: FRANCE: Minimalism rises again on Lagerfeld's catwalk.
newsitem.headline: Minimalism rises again on Lagerfeld's catwalk.

text.p: Just as it seemed that minimalism was going out of style, German designer Karl Lagerfeld put it back on to the catwalk on Friday in his signature ready-to-wear collection.

Lagerfeld dressed his anaemic models, their eyes reddened and hair coiffed in a madwoman's do, in variations on the fluid jersey dress -- slim, stretchy garments in chocolate, coral or anthracite with the intricate seaming and asymmetric hems of that receding generation of northern designers .
A momentary splash of colour after the first quarter of an hour came in a sunburst doeskin halter dress and vinyl alligator skin bomber jackets.

But then it was back to a one-track fashion vision, this time with sheer webby crochets -- ankle-length slip dresses, midriffs over minis, or bathrobe jackets -- that clung to ever more skeletal bodies. The monotony was punctuated twice -- by a spongy mint jacket, then a yellow tanktop over knickers, this Spring-Summer season's new discovery.
Coming from a man with a reputation as a trend-setter, it was a disappointing show, lacking the variety and unpredictability that were long Lagerfeld's forte.

Fortunately for Emanuel Ungaro, wearable clothes have become a novelty in a fashion world increasingly focused on crowd-pleasing spectacle. With a weak domestic market and a strong franc making exports costly, Ungaro kept his sights on the bottom line.
His spring florals, snakeskin coats and nubby, pointillist tweeds were just the thing for high-powered urban executives.

Ungaro kept those wealthy Middle Eastern customers and the glitzy new Russian rich in mind as well, offering up chiffon ensembles in bubblegum, electric chartreuse and peach, edged with silver and gold lace and flecked with strass, or eye-catching fuchsia suits over sunset chiffons.
John Galliano dazzled the Paris fashion crowd on Thursday night with a spellbinding display of designs staged as a gypsy gathering in an abandoned Paris wine warehouse.

Fires burned in rusty barrels and ragged clothes hung out to dry as Paris's beau monde soiled their designer shoes tripping on tyres and other rubbish to reach the warehouse in a Parisian no-man's land.
Inside, acrobats flipped about and a gypsy band chanted as supermodels sashayed out in tiny dresses of exquisite Chantilly or leather bikers' suits adorned with Indian mirror embroidery.
Then out came the gypsy costumes: fringed Russian shawls stitched into striking bias-cut gowns or a satin belly dancer's ensemble trimmed with astonishingly delicate petit-point.
Each piece was a masterpiece, from foamy lace blouses and thigh-high embroidered boots to a magnificent fortune teller's dress with tiers of dark silk edged in ribbons and gold brocade.
It all seemed too magical for real life, but Be Bilzerian, owner of a specialty store in Boston, Massachusetts, insisted that Galliano's clothes did go beyond the catwalk.
"Everyone wants to look like a diva for a night," she said. "You don't buy these kinds of clothes, or a Hermes pocketbook, if you're worried about the price."
Kalman Ruttenstein of Bloomingdale was more effusive.
"Every couple of years there's a special moment in fashion, and this sure was one. Any weaker word than spectacular would be wrong," he said.
Galliano's theatrics could have come at no better time.

In the front row sat the new owner of his house Bernard Arnault, head of luxury giant LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton, who is expected next week to announce Galliano's appointment as designer at Christian Dior, another LVMH asset.
